column1: # The sockets the retired server binds, the old backlog. Earlier research
# records the SAN requirement and not the topology it applies to, and an earlier
# study called this gap a blocker.
# Columns: listener, the key that gives its port, that port, the key that turns
# TLS on, the key that names its certificate, what it answers. A cell of -
# means the listener takes no certificate.
# Read from a run, not from the source. The binary was built with CGO_ENABLED=1
# inside golang:1.26 and started as `prusa-connect serve` against the
# shipped config/config.yaml on 2026-08-29. Four listening sockets appeared in
# /proc/net/tcp: 0050, 075B, 075C and 1F90, which are 80, 1883, 1884 and 8080.
# The two HTTP listeners were then given a certificate each and dialled with
# `openssl s_client`.
# What the run found:
#   Two HTTP listeners, each with its own certificate and its own floor. Port
#   8080 answered with an RSA 2048 certificate and refused TLS 1.2 outright,
#   with alert 70. Port 80 answered with an ECDSA P-256 certificate and
#   completed a TLS 1.2 handshake on ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384, which is the
#   one suite xBuddy firmware offers.
#   Firmware is configured against the printer listener and never the API one.
#   The server says so itself: GET /api/server/info answered printer_port 80,
#   ws_url ws://<host>:80/p/ws and register_url http://<host>:80/p/register.
#   The two MQTT sockets are the internal broker and they carry no certificate.
#   mqtt.mode external replaces both with a dial to somebody else's broker.
#   The core binds one listener by default, core.api.addr, and printers dial it.
#   A deployment that wants a second socket sets the connector's own
#   listener.addr. So three of
#   these four have no counterpart in the core, and docker/server/server.local.yml
#   publishes one port where this server wanted three.
